chunks: "There are a few layers of offload, from cheap to heavy.

The simplest is using peripheral hardware properly: timers generate PWM and measure pulses, UARTs and SPI controllers have FIFOs, and ADCs trigger from timers, so the CPU isn't toggling pins or watching a clock.
Next is interrupts instead of polling, so the CPU can do other work or sleep until something happens.
Then DMA: a DMA controller moves blocks between a peripheral and memory on its own, and interrupts the CPU only when a buffer is full.
For compute, you can use coprocessors and accelerators: a hardware floating-point unit, a crypto engine, a DSP, a GPU for parallel graphics or ML, or a second core.
What can you do in parallel?

Independent things: DMA transfers while the CPU computes on another buffer, which is double buffering; peripherals running autonomously; multiple cores on independent threads; accelerators on separate frames.
The trade-offs are real. Hardware costs area and power and is less flexible than software.
Everything shares the memory bus, so a DMA stream or GPU can slow the CPU through contention.
There's setup and synchronization overhead, so offloading a tiny task can be slower than just doing it.
You need cache coherence or explicit flushes, plus more complex software and verification.
And Amdahl's law says that offloading a part of the program only helps up to that part's share of the runtime."
